power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

info.title: Electronic Health Record-Based Machine-Learning for Cardiac Arrhythmia Identification in Adults with High-Risk Chronic Disease: Model Development and Validation Study

text.text: Objective: To develop and internally evaluate an electronic health record (EHR)-based machine-learning model to identify patients more likely to receive a documented cardiac arrhythmia diagnosis.

We retrospectively evaluated EHR data (2018-2025) from one healthcare organization among adults with type 2 diabetes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chronic kidney disease, or coronary artery disease.
Logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost were compared.
XGBoost was selected using internal validation, reduced to 30 features using Shapley additive explanations, and evaluated in a holdout set with data ending one day before the index date.
Sensitivity analyses excluded information recorded within 30, 90, or 180 days before the index date.
An atrial fibrillation/flutter-specific analysis compared XGBoost with CHARGE-AF and HARMS 2 -AF.
Results: Among 30,356 patients, 6,835 (22.5%) had a qualifying arrhythmia diagnosis.

In 3,051 holdout patients, XGBoost achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.894 (95% CI 0.879-0.908) and an area under the precision-recall curve of 0.792 (95% CI 0.763-0.822).
At a 0.5 threshold, sensitivity was 0.564, specificity 0.971, and precision 0.857.
AUROC remained 0.896-0.897 across earlier cutoffs.
In the common score-calculable atrial fibrillation/flutter subset (𝑛 = 2,436), AUROCs were 0.883 for XGBoost, 0.712 for CHARGE-AF, and 0.554 for HARMS 2 -AF.
Conclusions: XGBoost demonstrated strong internal discrimination for documented arrhythmias.
External validation and prospective evaluation are needed to assess generalizability and clinical utility.

Cardiac arrhythmias comprise a heterogeneous group of abnormalities in cardiac impulse formation and conduction, ranging from asymptomatic or intermittent rhythm disturbances to clinically consequential tachyarrhythmias and conduction disorders. [1, 2, 3] Because many arrhythmias are episodic or minimally symptomatic, diagnosis may occur incidentally or only after patients develop symptoms or related cardiovascular complications. [3] The burden of arrhythmia is particularly relevant among patients with chronic cardiometabolic and cardiopulmonary disease.

To develop and internally evaluate an EHR-based ML model to identify, among adults with a T2DM, COPD, CKD or CAD comorbidity, those patients with a greater likelihood of subsequently receiving a documented cardiac arrhythmia diagnosis in their available EHR data.

We compared logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost and evaluated the selected model on a held-out test set using records available up to one day before the index date, with sensitivity analyses excluding the final 30, 90, and 180 days.
As a secondary analysis, XGBoost was compared with CHARGE-AF and HARMS 2 -AF after restricting the outcome to AF. [12, 13]  >MATERIALS AND METHODS
text.formatted: As a secondary analysis, XGBoost was compared with CHARGE-AF and HARMS 2 -AF after restricting the outcome to AF. <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13]</ref> <head n="2." >MATERIALS AND METHODS</head>

text.text: We conducted a retrospective cohort study to develop and internally validate an ML model for identifying patients at elevated risk for clinically documented cardiac arrhythmia.
Documented arrhythmia, defined by ICD-10-CM diagnosis codes, [19] served as the prediction target and as a proxy for the presence of arrhythmia for supervised model training.
text.formatted: Documented arrhythmia, defined by ICD-10-CM diagnosis codes, <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref> served as the prediction target and as a proxy for the presence of arrhythmia for supervised model training.

text.text: The intended use is to identify patients without a documented qualifying arrhythmia who may warrant prioritization for further clinical evaluation.
The model output is intended for risk stratification and should not be interpreted as establishing an arrhythmia diagnosis.
All analyses were performed using EHR data from Desert Oasis Healthcare, covering the period 2018 through 2025.
The machine-learning models were developed and the associated analyses were performed as part of a healthcare provider's quality improvement activities under a business associate agreement.
Subsequent interpretation and reporting of the existing results did not involve protected health information (PHI) or require access to source EHR records or patient-level datasets.
This subsequent work involved no patient recruitment, direct patient contact, or changes to clinical care.
The BRANY Institutional Review Board reviewed the study protocol and determined the study to be exempt under 45 CFR § 46.104(d)(4)(ii) (protocol LH-ARR-001; BRANY IRB file 26-12-716-2819).
Individual informed consent was not required for this exempt secondary research.

Eligible patients were aged 18 years or older and had, before any qualifying arrhythmia diagnosis, at least one qualifying diagnosis of T2DM (E11), COPD (J40-J44), CKD (N18), or CAD (I20-I25), including all subcodes within these categories.

The primary outcome was a documented qualifying cardiac arrhythmia diagnosis in the EHR within one of the following ICD-10-CM categories: I44 (atrioventricular and left bundle-branch block), I47 (paroxysmal tachycardia), I48 (AF), and I49 (other cardiac arrhythmias), including all subcodes within each category.

Patients with one or more qualifying codes were classified as arrhythmia-positive, with the earliest qualifying diagnosis determining the primary arrhythmia category; patients meeting the comorbidity eligibility criterion but without any qualifying arrhythmia code were classified as arrhythmia-negative.
For each patient, the available EHR observation period was defined using diagnosis, vital-sign, and laboratory records.
Arrhythmia-positive patients were indexed at the date of the earliest recorded qualifying arrhythmia diagnosis.
For arrhythmia-negative patients, the index date was set to last observed clinical encounter.
Prior to model development, 10% of patients were randomly assigned to a final holdout test set that was excluded from all model training, tuning, and internal validation.
The remaining 90% of patients were partitioned into training and internal validation sets using stratified random sampling to preserve arrhythmia prevalence.
The training, internal validation, and holdout sets included 21,844, 5,461, and 3,051 patients, respectively, with similar arrhythmia prevalence across partitions (Supplementary Table S1).
text.formatted: The training, internal validation, and holdout sets included 21,844, 5,461, and 3,051 patients, respectively, with similar arrhythmia prevalence across partitions (Supplementary Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S1</ref>).

text.text: Features were restricted to data before each patient's cutoff, randomly set 1-180 days before the index date during development.
Primary holdout evaluation used a 1-day cutoff, with 30-, 90-, and 180-day cutoffs for temporal sensitivity analyses.
Candidate predictors were derived from demographic, diagnostic, laboratory, and vital-sign/anthropometric EHR domains.

Diagnostic features and corresponding ICD-10-CM codes are provided in Supplementary Table S2, laboratory features and Logical Observation Identifiers Names and Codes (LOINC) identifiers in Supplementary Table S3, and vital-sign and anthropometric features in Supplementary Table S4. [20] Race and ethnicity were harmonized into two categories for modeling: White, non-Hispanic and Other racial and ethnic groups.

text.text: Patients were classified as White, non-Hispanic only when both criteria were recorded; all others were grouped as Other racial and ethnic groups.

Laboratory, vital-sign, and anthropometric measurements were standardized and cleaned by harmonizing units according to Unified Code for Units of Measure (UCUM) conventions, [21] and excluding values outside prespecified biologically plausible ranges; detailed coding and range specifications are provided in Supplementary Tables S3 and S4.
text.formatted: Laboratory, vital-sign, and anthropometric measurements were standardized and cleaned by harmonizing units according to Unified Code for Units of Measure (UCUM) conventions, <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref> and excluding values outside prespecified biologically plausible ranges; detailed coding and range specifications are provided in Supplementary Tables <ref type="table">S3</ref> and <ref type="table">S4</ref>.

text.text: For each variable, we calculated the median of all available measurements (_MEDIAN); a long-term normalized change, defined as the difference between the last and first values divided by elapsed days (_NORM_DELTA); an analogous normalized change restricted to the 547 days preceding the final measurement (_NORM_DELTA_18MO); and the mean and median of the three most recent measurements (_MEAN_LAST3 and _MEDIAN_LAST3).
When only one measurement was available in the relevant window, normalized change was assigned a value of zero.
After feature creation and preprocessing, the initial modeling dataset included 128 candidate features before feature selection and model training.

Missing laboratory, vital sign, and anthropometric features were median-imputed using feature-specific medians estimated from the training subset and applied unchanged to the validation and holdout sets to prevent information leakage.
Distributions and pre-imputation missingness of final XGBoost features are reported in Supplementary Table S5.
text.formatted: Distributions and pre-imputation missingness of final XGBoost features are reported in Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S5</ref>.

text.text: Three supervised learning algorithms were evaluated: logistic regression, [22] random forest, [23] and gradient boosted decision trees implemented using XGBoost. [24] Logistic regression was included as an interpretable linear baseline, while random forest and XGBoost were evaluated to capture potential nonlinear relationships and interactions among clinical features.
text.formatted: Three supervised learning algorithms were evaluated: logistic regression, <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref> random forest, <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref> and gradient boosted decision trees implemented using XGBoost. <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24]</ref> Logistic regression was included as an interpretable linear baseline, while random forest and XGBoost were evaluated to capture potential nonlinear relationships and interactions among clinical features.

text.text: The data used for model development was partitioned as described above.
All models were trained and assessed within the same development framework, using performance on the internal validation set to guide model selection.
Hyperparameter tuning was performed for logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost using exhaustive grid search with 3-fold stratified cross-validation on the training set.
AUROC was used as the optimization metric.
The hyperparameter search space is provided in Supplementary Table S6.
text.formatted: The hyperparameter search space is provided in Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S6</ref>.

text.text: For each model, the hyperparameter configuration with the highest mean cross-validated AUROC was selected.
The three tuned models were then evaluated on the internal validation set to compare performance during model development.
AUROC was used as the primary scoring metric, with additional consideration given to precision, specificity, and sensitivity.
XGBoost showed the highest AUROC and area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) and was therefore selected for feature reduction and final holdout evaluation.

After hyperparameter tuning, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) values [25] were calculated across patients in the training data to estimate each feature's contribution to the XGBoost model's predictions.
text.formatted: After hyperparameter tuning, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) values <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref> were calculated across patients in the training data to estimate each feature's contribution to the XGBoost model's predictions.

text.text: Features were ranked according to mean absolute SHAP value in the training data.
The 30 highest-ranked features were retained to produce a more parsimonious final model and facilitate interpretation.
The choice of 30 features was pragmatic rather than derived from a formal feature-count optimization procedure.

The XGBoost model with the top 30 features and the selected hyperparameter configuration was then trained on the combined training and internal validation sets, representing 90% of the full study cohort.
The final XGBoost model was evaluated on the prespecified holdout set using a 0.5 probability threshold.
Performance was assessed using AUROC, AUPRC, sensitivity, specificity, precision, negative predictive value (NPV), F1 score, accuracy, and Brier score.
The 30-, 90-, and 180-day cutoffs were evaluated as temporal sensitivity analyses.
Final model performance was also examined separately across the four arrhythmia categories defined by the earliest qualifying ICD-10-CM diagnosis within I44, I47, I48, or I49, including all subcodes.
Model interpretability was assessed using SHAP values for the final XGBoost model.
For the 30 retained features, SHAP beeswarm plots and mean absolute SHAP importance rankings were generated to visualize feature contributions.
These plots were used to examine the direction and magnitude of individual feature contributions to the model output.
SHAP values were interpreted as model attributions and not as causal effects or estimates of absolute clinical risk.
Subgroup analyses were conducted to assess whether final model performance was consistent across clinically and demographically relevant groups.
Subgroups included recorded gender, race/ethnicity, and age.
Recorded gender was evaluated as female and male, and race/ethnicity was evaluated using the two-level race/ethnicity feature.
Age-based subgroup performance was evaluated using four categories: 18-39, 40-64, 65-79, and ≥80 years.

Fairness was evaluated using demographic parity difference and equalized odds difference, implemented with the Fairlearn library. [26] These metrics were used to assess between-group differences in positive prediction rates and error-rate patterns, respectively.
text.formatted: Fairness was evaluated using demographic parity difference and equalized odds difference, implemented with the Fairlearn library. <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26]</ref> These metrics were used to assess between-group differences in positive prediction rates and error-rate patterns, respectively.

text.text: Values closer to zero indicate more similar model behavior across groups.
CHARGE-AF and HARMS 2 -AF were calculated as secondary clinical benchmarks for the AF component of the study outcome.
The published CHARGE-AF equation was used to generate a 5-year absolute risk estimate for AF, whereas HARMS 2 -AF was evaluated as an integer point-based risk score.

Because both scores were developed for AF prediction, this comparison was restricted to patients with diagnoses within I48, including all subcodes, as positive cases and patients from the primary arrhythmia-negative cohort as controls; patients whose qualifying outcome was a non-I48 arrhythmia were excluded.
All three approaches were evaluated in the same subset of holdout patients for whom both clinical scores were calculable.
Discrimination was assessed using AUROC and AUPRC.

Threshold-dependent performance was additionally reported at a probability threshold of 0.5 for XGBoost, CHARGE-AF 5-year risk thresholds of 2.5% and 5%, [27] and a HARMS 2 -AF threshold of ≥5 points. [13] The common score-calculable comparison cohort was additionally characterized relative to the full holdout population with respect to demographic characteristics and outcome composition (Supplementary Table S7).

text.text: In this retrospective EHR-based cohort study of adults with T2DM, COPD, CKD, or CAD, we developed and internally evaluated a ML model for identifying patients at elevated risk of clinically documented cardiac arrhythmia.

The final XGBoost model used 30 SHAP-selected features spanning demographic, diagnostic, laboratory, vital sign, and anthropometric domains and demonstrated strong discrimination in the primary held-out test set.
Model discrimination remained stable when data from the final 30, 90, and 180 days before the index or censoring date were excluded, supporting robustness across a range of prediction lead times.
Among the three candidate models, XGBoost had the highest discrimination.

Its AUROC was also numerically higher than that reported in several prior EHR-based studies of AF and broader cardiac dysrhythmia prediction, [14, 15, 16, 17, 18] although cross-study comparisons should be interpreted cautiously given differences in study populations, outcome definitions, prediction horizons, feature sets, and validation designs.

text.text: The principal distinction of the present study is its evaluation of a broader documented-arrhythmia outcome among adults with T2DM, COPD, CKD, or CAD, using longitudinal EHR information.
It additionally provides an AF-specific head-to-head comparison with established clinical risk scores in a common calculable subset.
Within the AF-specific comparison, XGBoost demonstrated greater discrimination than CHARGE-AF and HARMS 2 -AF.

CHARGE-AF and HARMS 2 -AF use a limited set of predefined clinical risk factors, whereas the XGBoost model incorporated a broader set of EHR-derived features, including longitudinal laboratory and vital-sign summaries.

CHARGE-AF was developed to estimate incident AF risk over a 5-year horizon, and HARMS 2 -AF was developed and externally validated for new-onset AF in community-based populations. [12, 13] XGBoost showed greater relative discrimination within this comorbidity-enriched cohort and serves as a secondary cohort-specific benchmark.

This distinction is relevant when applying prediction approaches to routinely collected EHR data, in which missingness and patterns of data collection are common methodological considerations. [28, 29] SHAP analysis provided insight into model predictions.

text.text: Age was the strongest contributor, consistent with the previously established increase in arrhythmia incidence, particularly AF, with advancing age. [30] Multiple hematologic and renal/metabolic measures, including platelet, hemoglobin, blood urea nitrogen, calcium, and chloride, were also influential.

text.text: Several highly ranked predictors represented time-standardized changes in laboratory measurements, indicating that the fitted model used longitudinal information in addition to static summaries.
SHAP does not, however, quantify the independent predictive value of longitudinal features.
Model performance was generally similar across recorded gender and race/ethnicity groups.
At the default threshold, between-group differences were smaller for recorded gender than for race/ethnicity.
The latter finding may reflect variation in outcome prevalence and healthcare utilization, [28, 29] which can influence feature availability and outcome documentation in EHRs.
text.formatted: The latter finding may reflect variation in outcome prevalence and healthcare utilization, <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[28,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">29]</ref> which can influence feature availability and outcome documentation in EHRs.

text.text: The two-level race/ethnicity classification also prevented more granular assessment.
Age-stratified performance was less stable in younger adults: only five positive cases were available among patients aged 18-39 years.
Performance in this subgroup therefore remains uncertain.

At the 0.5 threshold, the model traded sensitivity for high specificity and precision, yielding a relatively small, enriched subgroup that could potentially be prioritized for further clinical evaluation.
The appropriate operating threshold would depend on the intended clinical workflow and the relative consequences of false-positive and false-negative predictions.
ICD-10-CM diagnoses served as the study outcome, and confirmation of an arrhythmia requires appropriate rhythm assessment and clinical interpretation.
Future prospective studies could evaluate model-guided rhythm assessment for earlier identification of clinically confirmed arrhythmia.

Together, these findings support further evaluation of longitudinal EHR-based ML risk identification for prioritizing clinical assessment in populations with cardiometabolic and cardiopulmonary disease burden.
This study has several limitations.
First, model development and evaluation were performed using data from a single healthcare organization.

A prespecified holdout set provided independent internal evaluation, but external validation is needed to assess transportability across populations, care settings, coding practices, and EHR data availability.

Second, the outcome was based on ICD-10-CM diagnosis codes rather than adjudicated electrocardiographic or rhythm-monitoring findings. [31] The first qualifying code may not represent biological disease onset, and some patients classified as negative may have had undocumented arrhythmias.
text.formatted: Second, the outcome was based on ICD-10-CM diagnosis codes rather than adjudicated electrocardiographic or rhythm-monitoring findings. <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[31]</ref> The first qualifying code may not represent biological disease onset, and some patients classified as negative may have had undocumented arrhythmias.

text.text: Positive labels may also reflect historical, miscoded, or unconfirmed diagnosis.
The results therefore represent prediction of documented arrhythmia rather than adjudicated incident arrhythmia.
Third, the index date differed by outcome status: first qualifying diagnosis for arrhythmia-positive patients and last encounter for arrhythmia-negative patients.
The study therefore did not estimate absolute arrhythmia risk from a common prediction time over a defined follow-up interval.

The temporal sensitivity analyses show that performance was not driven solely by immediately pre-diagnostic information but do not remove possible differences in observation history or healthcare utilization.

Fourth, routinely collected EHR data are subject to informative presence and missingness. [28, 29, 32] Patients with greater healthcare utilization generate more measurements and have more opportunities for an arrhythmia diagnosis to be recorded.

text.text: Median imputation enabled complete scoring but did not capture informative missingness, while longitudinal summaries may reflect differences in measurement density.
Finally, the reported 0.5 probability threshold was not optimized for clinical utility.
Future external and prospective evaluation could assess discrimination, calibration, workflow-specific thresholds, and clinical utility including decision-curve analysis. [33]

Discrimination remained similar after progressively excluding more proximal EHR information, and the model showed greater discrimination than CHARGE-AF and HARMS 2 -AF in a secondary AF-specific benchmark.
